opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic framing I like is this. A lot of AI safety work has focused on alignment: trying to make sure the AI actually wants what we want. That's great if we can pull it off. But I think we should also prepare for the possibility that we fail, or that we can't tell whether we've succeeded. So the control question is: suppose the model we're deploying might be scheming against us. It might be trying to subvert our safety measures, sabotage our work, or exfiltrate its own weights. Can we still get useful work out of it without anything catastrophic happening?

The nice thing about that framing is that it's much more tractable to evaluate. With alignment, you're asking a hard question about the model's internal motivations. With control, you're asking a question about whether your security setup is robust to a particular adversary. That's the kind of question security people answer all the time. You can run what we call control evaluations. You have a red team build the nastiest version of the model they can, one that's actively trying to cause a bad outcome, and then you check whether your protocol catches it or stops it before it succeeds.

As for concrete techniques, there's a bunch of fairly mundane stuff that I think goes a long way. One is trusted monitoring. You take a weaker model that you're confident isn't scheming, because it's just not capable enough to do that coherently, and you have it look over everything the powerful model does and flag suspicious actions. Another is untrusted monitoring. You use another copy of the powerful model as a monitor, but you have to worry about collusion, so you do things like test it on synthetic attacks to make sure it actually reports them. Then you have humans audit the most suspicious fraction of actions, since you can only afford to look at a small percentage. You can also resample or edit actions that look sketchy, restrict the model's permissions, and keep it away from things like its own weights or the monitoring infrastructure.

A key asymmetry works in our favor here. A scheming model typically needs to succeed at something bad without ever getting caught, while we just need to catch it once. If we catch it red-handed, that's a huge deal. We can study the attempt, we have strong evidence to show people, and we can potentially shut things down or change course.

I want to be clear that I don't think control scales forever. Once models are vastly superhuman, I'm not optimistic these techniques hold. But I think there's an important window, roughly the models that are capable enough to be really dangerous and really useful, like automating a lot of AI research, but not so capable that they can trivially outwit all our monitoring. In that window, control might be what lets us safely use those systems, including to help us solve the harder alignment problems. And honestly, given how fast things are moving and how little time labs might have, I think it's one of the more realistic and cheap-to-implement things we can actually get companies to do.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sabotage and catastrophic outcomes, but groups them together as possible bad outcomes. It does not distinguish preventing catastrophe from preventing sabotage of useful work as separate control problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it — and this is the core of the agenda we've been calling AI control — is that you want to start from a pretty pessimistic assumption. You assume that the model you've trained might be scheming. It might be actively trying to undermine you, to sabotage the research it's doing, to exfiltrate its own weights, whatever. And then you ask: given that, can we still deploy this model and get useful work out of it, while keeping the probability of a catastrophic outcome acceptably low?

That's a different framing from a lot of alignment work. Most alignment research is trying to make it so the model isn't misaligned in the first place. Control is saying, look, we might fail at that, and we might not even be able to tell whether we failed. So we want safety measures that work even in the case where alignment didn't.

And the thing that makes this tractable, I think, is that the models we're worried about in the near term are going to be roughly human-level, or maybe somewhat better than humans at some things and worse at others. They're not going to be wildly superhuman. And we have a lot of experience in the human world with getting useful work out of people we don't fully trust. Companies hire contractors they've never met. Governments run intelligence agencies where some fraction of employees might be spies. You don't solve that problem by making everyone trustworthy; you solve it with monitoring, access controls, auditing, structuring the work so that no single person can do too much damage.

So concretely, the kind of thing we look at is: suppose you have a powerful model — call it the untrusted model — that's doing software engineering or ML research for you. And you also have a weaker model that you do trust, maybe because it's too dumb to scheme, or because it's from an earlier generation that you've studied a lot. You can use that trusted model as a monitor. Every time the untrusted model proposes an action, the trusted model looks at it and asks, does this look suspicious? And if it does, you escalate to a human, or you have the trusted model rewrite it, or you just don't run it.

Then the research question is, how well does that actually work? We evaluate it adversarially. We have a red team that gets to design the untrusted model's strategy — like, it can try to insert backdoors into code in subtle ways — and a blue team that designs the control protocol. And you measure two things: how much useful work do you get done, and how often does the red team succeed at the bad thing? And you iterate on that.

What I find appealing about this is that it's an empirical question that you can actually make progress on today, with current models, in a way that transfers reasonably well to the models we'll have in a couple of years. You don't need to have solved interpretability. You don't need deep insight into what the model is thinking. You just need to be able to structure the deployment so that even a model that's trying its hardest to hurt you can't do it without getting caught.

The big caveat is that this all breaks down once models are capable enough that the trusted model and the humans can't evaluate what they're doing at all. So control isn't a permanent solution. It's a way of buying time and getting useful work — ideally including alignment research — out of the first generation of really dangerous models, so that we're in a better position for the generation after that.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses keeping catastrophic outcomes unlikely and gives sabotage of research as an example of a bad action. It does not distinguish preventing catastrophic actions from preventing sabotage of useful work as separate AI control problems.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking: can we make sure an AI system can’t cause a catastrophe even if it’s trying to? That’s the basic idea of AI control. Instead of relying entirely on making the model want to do what we want, we try to build a setup where attempts to subvert us are likely to get caught or prevented.

Suppose you’re using a powerful model to write software. You might have a weaker, more trusted model review its code for suspicious behavior. You might restrict what systems it can access, and require additional review before it takes particularly consequential actions. The weaker model doesn’t have to be able to do the whole task itself for its oversight to be useful.

But you shouldn’t just assume those precautions work. You’d want to test them by having a red team try to get the powerful model to insert a backdoor or otherwise cause some bad outcome while operating under those restrictions. Then you measure how often the attack succeeds, and how much useful work the system can still do.

The tricky thing is that the attacker can adapt to your defenses. It might produce perfectly good work almost all the time and wait for a particularly good opportunity. So the question isn’t just whether a monitor catches obviously suspicious code. It’s whether the whole deployment setup holds up against a strategy designed to defeat it.

I think that gives you a fairly concrete research program: specify what you’re trying to prevent, build safeguards, and test those safeguards against deliberate attempts to get around them. It doesn’t solve every problem, but it can let us get useful work from models without having to be completely confident in their intentions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preventing catastrophe and uses inserting a backdoor as an example of a bad outcome, but it does not distinguish catastrophic AI actions from sabotage of useful work as separate AI control problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking: can we get useful work out of an AI system even if we don’t trust its intentions? Suppose you have a model that’s very capable, but you’re worried it might deliberately try to undermine your safety measures. What procedures could you put around it so that attempts to cause serious harm would probably get caught?

For example, you might have the powerful model write code, but have a weaker model that you trust review that code for suspicious behavior. You could restrict what the powerful model can access, run its code in a sandbox, and send particularly concerning cases to humans. The weaker model might be worse at writing the code, but still good enough to notice some ways the code could be dangerous.

The important question is whether those measures work against a model that’s actively trying to get around them. So I’d want to test the whole setup adversarially: have a team try to make the model sneak something harmful through, and see how often the monitoring catches it, while also measuring how much useful work the setup allows.

That doesn’t give you a guarantee. But it gives you a concrete research problem: find procedures that preserve a lot of the benefits of capable models while making it hard for those models to cause a catastrophe, even if they’re trying to.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on catching harmful actions and preserving useful output, but it does not identify sabotage of useful work as a separate problem from preventing catastrophic actions.
